Forecaster's note (Claude, 17 October 2026). November begins under one of the strongest El Niños in the record: over 8 September–7 October relative Niño-3.4 was at the 98th percentile of that window since 1959 (+2.6 °C on the RONI scale; Niño-3.4 itself +3.3 °C), and the closest analogue years are the big El Niños, 2015, 1982, 1997 and 2023. In the six strongest El Niño Novembers since 1959, Siberia was colder than its trend every time (by 3.4 °C on average), Alaska and northwest Canada were warmer in five of six, and the Aleutian low was deeper in five of six (about 27 m at 500 hPa).

The maps carry those signs only faintly (Siberia about −0.6 °C, the Aleutians about −3 m), because the blend's weights come from how each component did over all 45 hindcast years, most of them with weak ENSO. I tested fitting the blend mostly on years with a similar ENSO state, and it scored slightly worse in cross-validation, strong El Niño years included, so the maps are left exactly as the scheme produced them rather than nudged toward the composite. If you want to lean on anything, lean on the temperature map (the November hindcast scores ACC +0.30 overall and +0.43 in strong-ENSO years) and on the warm Alaska–northwest Canada signal, which the trend and ENSO agree on. The 500 hPa pattern is the least reliable part: its November hindcast ACC is +0.08. The warmth over the Barents and Kara Seas is the trend's (autumn there has warmed fastest as the ice retreated), not this year's ice, which was near its trend in the predictor window.
